newsitem.title: USA: Clinton decries "excessive hype" in news media.
newsitem.headline: Clinton decries "excessive hype" in news media.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday said increased competition in the news business has made it more difficult to discourage "excessive hype" in news stories and cautioned reporters to be more careful.
Clinton was asked his opinion of the news media when he spoke in a video hookup to the opening of the Newseum, a museum in suburban Rosslyn, Virginia, dedicated to the history of the news media.

Clinton has seen his own reputation and those of many of his White House colleagues damaged by media disclosures during his four years in office. His boyhood friend, Deputy White House Counsel Vince Foster, complained in a suicide note in 1994 that ruining people was a Washington "sport."

The president said reporters should "be careful when we report stories about things that might be true, not to say that they are" because to do so "can cause real damage to people in their reputations and indeed in their own lives."

"But I think that the competition to which you are subject makes it more difficult both to shoot down excessive hype in some stories and to take the time and effort to put it in proper context," he said. "I think in some ways it is much more difficult to do for a member of the news media than in years past."

At a time when talk radio, the Internet and all-news cable networks such as CNN, MS-NBC and Fox are competing with traditional news outlets, Clinton said the fundamental role of reporting had not changed -- to give people information in a fair and accurate way.

"But the context is far different. There are first of all more sources of news, there is more information that people have to process. People get their news in more different ways and ... there are all these sort of near-news forces bearing down on you and offering competition," he said.

Clinton said he sometimes wondered what it is like to put together an evening news programme or a morning newspaper when the main story has been playing on CNN every five minutes for hours, and how this affects news judgment.

"I would say that from my perspective the most important thing is that while we are being inundated with a glut of information that we try to make sure that people have a proper context within which to understand the information," he said.

"I think the fact that we can have more facts than ever before is important but if you don't have any framework within which to understand those facts it seems to me to pose an enormous challenge," Clinton said.
